title: What are we paying attention to?
author: Marcus Luther
summary: Marcus Luther begins with his great-uncle's funeral, where one daughter's charge to pay attention to people became a lens on the current direction of schooling. He argues that the recurring urgency narrative around test results, most recently the PISA reading headlines, pulls the attention of decision-makers toward spreadsheets and away from students. Luther then turns the critique on himself, admitting that as a data-minded, bell-to-bell teacher he has sometimes let scripted urgency crowd out genuine attention to the people in his room. He lists the practices he has used this year to redirect attention, from reading and sharing back student surveys to pulse checks, celebrating beautiful sentences, and peer nominations. The essay ends by framing attention as an expression of values and ultimately an act of hope, followed by four recommended pieces from other writers.
points: Luther describes a cycle in which test results produce calamity headlines, think pieces, and policy, only to repeat with the next release.
He argues that pressure for rigorous materials and scripted pacing can lead teachers themselves to stop attending to the students in front of them.
Students, he notes, are paying attention to how teachers pay attention, so the spreadsheet focus sends exactly the wrong signal.
Concrete practices include index-card surveys shared back with students, narrative writing time, pulse checks, sentence celebrations, and peer affirmations.
Paying attention is framed as an expression of what we value and as an act of hope amid the heaviness of teaching.
quotes: When I think about paying attention to people, the last thing I think about is staring at a spreadsheet and scrutinizing test scores.

This is the cycle we cannot seem to break in recent years, isn’t it? Test results come out, headlines regurgitate calamity, think-pieces ensue and escalate into policy, and just as the dust settles…another set of test results take to the headlines.

The eyes of those making decisions seem to be much more fixated upon spreadsheets than students, and rather than decision-makers closing the distance between themselves and the classroom to interrupt that spreadsheet fixation, there is instead increasing pressure on teachers to look away from the students who are literally seated in front of us.
Amidst that increasing pressure, I think, just maybe, sometimes we give in. Sometimes we start paying attention to what those outside of classrooms want us to pay attention to.
Something that I’ve been thinking about a lot over these opening weeks of school: our students are paying attention to how we are paying attention.
After all, the act of paying attention is an expression of what we value—both in what we choose to pay attention to as well as what we neglect to attend to.
We pay attention to people because there is good to be found in people, and therefore the act of paying attention is more than just a signal.
